theme: Defilement; the Syrophoenician woman; Peter’s confession
readingInstruction: Read Mark 7:1-8:38. Jesus teaches about what defiles, heals a Gentile woman’s daughter, feeds four thousand, and then asks his disciples, “Who do you say that I am?” This is the turning point of the Gospel. Read Peter’s confession and what follows slowly.
settingTheScene: Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem to challenge Jesus about ceremonial washing. He turns the conversation to the heart. Then he travels north into Gentile territory, Tyre, Sidon, and the Decapolis, and heals Gentiles. Mark 8:27-30 is the center of the Gospel. The first half asks, who is this? The second half answers, the Christ who must suffer.
observation: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (7:6).
“There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him” (7:15).
“Yes, Lord; even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs” (7:28).
“He has done all things well. He even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak” (7:37).
“But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Christ” (8:29).
“And he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed, and after three days rise again” (8:31).
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me” (8:34).
“For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?” (8:36).
interpretation:
The Pharisees ask why Jesus’ disciples eat with unwashed hands. Jesus quotes Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” They have set aside the commandment of God to hold to human tradition. Then he teaches the crowd that it is not what goes into a person that defiles him but what comes out of the heart: evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, covetousness. The problem is not external but internal. Mark adds a parenthetical comment: “Thus he declared all foods clean.” The Old Testament dietary laws, which marked Israel off from the nations, have fulfilled their purpose.

Jesus goes to Tyre, where a Syrophoenician woman, a Gentile, begs him to cast a demon out of her daughter. He says, “Let the children be fed first,” meaning Israel has priority in the history of salvation. She answers with great faith and wit: “Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” Jesus says, “For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter.” She would not be turned away. Then he heals a deaf man, and the crowd says, “He has done all things well.” He feeds four thousand, probably Gentiles, and warns the disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees.

Then comes the turning point. At Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks, “Who do people say that I am?” They give the answers: John, Elijah, one of the prophets. Then, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answers, “You are the Christ.” This is the first time any human in Mark names Jesus rightly. And Jesus immediately begins to teach what kind of Christ he is: one who must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise again.

Peter takes him aside and rebukes him. Jesus turns, looks at his disciples, and says to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” Peter wanted a Messiah without a cross. Jesus insists on the cross, and calls everyone who follows him to the same road: “Let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.” For whoever loses his life for the sake of Jesus and the gospel will save it. “For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?”
connection: Isaiah 29:13 is the verse Jesus quotes. Leviticus 11 gives the dietary laws, and Acts 10:9-16 and Romans 14:14 show that they are no longer binding. Jeremiah 17:9 says the heart is deceitful. Isaiah 35:5-6 promises the deaf will hear. Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 53 point to the rejected, suffering Messiah. Luke 9:23-25 and Matthew 16:24-26 are parallels to the call to take up the cross. Galatians 2:20 says we have been crucified with Christ.
application:
Ask whether your heart is far from God even as your lips honor him. Confess it.

Take Peter’s confession as your own: “You are the Christ.” Then ask whether you are willing to follow the Christ who suffers.

Learn from the Syrophoenician woman’s persistence in prayer.
prayerPrompts: Confess who you believe Jesus is.
Ask him to purify your heart.
Thank him for hearing people like the Syrophoenician woman.
